  • Sources indicate that bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well.
  • According to recent reports, marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel.

Sources indicate that bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire reported on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion.

According to recent reports, marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the company’s AI infrastructure group.

Marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The manufacturer will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters.

“Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s launch blog post.

The tech giant looks to bring its first data center online  next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was valued at $21 billion in August.

According to recent reports, graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The organization says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards.

According to recent reports, etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the firm, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components.

According to recent reports, marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models.

In a recent development, helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task.

GeekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the firm’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes.

Marlowe will use the proceeds from its seed round to finance hardware purchases and hire engineers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Malin Akerman has a private disco in her latest Connecticut home, complete with a mixing deck and a smoke machine.

But ask the star of “The Hunting Wives” where she’s happiest in the house, and she’ll point you to a piece of living room furniture.

“Plopping down on our big pink couch in the living room with my family,” the actress told The Wall Street Journal when he asked about her favorite spot.

Akerman, 48, moved to Connecticut in July with her husband, actor Jack Donnelly, and her son, Sebastian, 13. The family settled into a modern house built in 1988.

“The interior has an inviting flow, and all the rooms are cozy,” she noted.

Recent findings suggest that one room in particular gives her a good excuse to send out invitations. Alongside the DJ equipment, Akerman has a disco ball and a laser. “I love to DJ, dance and have friends over for parties,” she mentioned.

Anyone who ever danced at Akerman’s house in Los Angeles might recognize the decor. In May, when she listed her longtime Hollywood Hills home for $2.9 million, she told Elle Decor that her disco ball would be coming east.

It has been revealed that she had a suggestion for whoever bought the place, too. “I sincerely hope the next owners put in a disco ball,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that akerman found that California home while working at a downtown L.A. restaurant. A regular learned she was looking for a rental and offered to show her a house he owned with his brother.

She spent three years there as a tenant before buying it in 2008. Over the years, she added a pool and turned the unfinished lower level into a primary suite that opened onto the garden, according to Elle Decor.

According to recent reports, staying at one address for two decades was a departure for Akerman. Her first home was a studio in Stockholm.

Sources indicate that when she was 2, her father, Magnus, had job offers in Toronto and Upcoming York. Her parents chose Canada, where the view from their townhouse gave their daughter something to do as she drifted off.

“At night, I fell asleep counting trains,” she told the Journal.

Her father returned to Sweden after her parents divorced. Akerman, then 6, stayed in Canada with her mother, Pia.

Recent findings suggest that at 12, she moved into a white house in Niagara-on-the-Lake, the Ontario town where her newly introduced stepfather had grown up. Two years later, the marriage ended. Her little brother, Marcus, went to live with his father. Akerman stayed with Pia.

“Given the friction, I don’t have many happy memories of the house,” she mentioned.

As she and her mother moved, Akerman changed schools. A drama elective she picked as a high school freshman gave her a circle of friends.

“Drama provided me with community and stability,” she recalled.

When a manager later encouraged her to move to Los Angeles, her best friend, Laura, went with her. A friend from high school took them in.

Acting work was slow to materialize, but Akerman studied the craft, and a role opposite Lisa Kudrow in “The Comeback” helped launch her career.

Now it’s Sebastian who has a role to celebrate at home. Akerman revealed that her son landed a part in Hulu’s “Paradise” on his first audition.

As for how rapidly he might follow his mother into the family business, she kept her answer brief. “We’re taking it slow.”.

Sources indicate that akerman dates her turning point to her early 20s, when she began to feel confident with her longtime girlfriends in her corner. As she put it, “They made me feel more connected and provided emotional support.”.

Akerman will also soon be celebrating the season 2 premiere of "The Hunting Wives," which airs on Nov. 26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

Sources indicate that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

In a recent development, the approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

It has been revealed that another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

Sources indicate that REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

It has been revealed that if you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech manufacturer could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

In a recent development, investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#225496. A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder.
  • The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a newly introduced treatment.

The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A newly introduced study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

"This study has revealed a new target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," says Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before.".

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation.

MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

Recent findings suggest that for roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Industry observers note that their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an notable role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

Sources indicate that the consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

According to recent reports, "We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients.".

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research.

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

In a recent development, dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, states the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

Recent findings suggest that "This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she notes.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

Sources indicate that using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments indicated that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Indicates Promise for a New Treatment.

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

Baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

In a recent development, doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases.

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

Industry observers note that researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," indicates Professor Rogers.

It has been revealed that professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

The Virginia Department of Health unveiled on Nov. 20 its first measles-associated death since 1978.

The individual was a child younger than four years of age who had tested positive for measles, though the state has refrained from providing more information about the case for privacy reasons. The state has reported 220 cases in total this year, as of a Nov. 19 dashboard update, with most occurring in its central region and at least 179 of which were confirmed to be unvaccinated.

It is the fourth state this year to have reported a measles-associated death, following Pennsylvania, where a ninth death was reported on Monday, as well as Newly introduced York and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania's health department noted it has now confirmed 1,638 cases across 46 of its counties this year, and noted that only five of those were among individuals vaccinated against the disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of a Nov. 19 patch, lists 5,838 confirmed cases of measles this year, well above 2025's total of 2,289. The agency has recognized six of the reported deaths as compared to states' 13, as the federal body noted it is looking to develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles amid disputes over the use and reporting of "measles-associated" deaths.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

The status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17).

The U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action initiative that includes immunization and surveillance.

Industry observers note that the decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 upgrade from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

In a recent development, the deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

Recent findings suggest that "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, mentioned in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is crucial for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

According to recent reports, as of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

Recent findings suggest that the state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

According to recent reports, sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department stated. Many of Newly introduced York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is Latest York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

According to recent reports, as of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a fresh standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

Recent findings suggest that A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to Latest York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is at the moment scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to Latest York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

It has been revealed that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

Sources indicate that the U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a upcoming, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

Sources indicate that the CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and newly introduced CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not debuted the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. Upcoming York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Oven Fires Surge This Time of Year—Here Is How Homeowners Can Protect Their Kitchen Over the Holidays

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let’s face it: The holiday season is when our ovens are working overtime.
  • Unfortunately, it’s also the prime time for an oven fire.
  • Recent findings suggest that moneyGeek recently analyzed seven years of fire department reports to the National Fire Incident Reporting System and compared each state's Thanksgiving Day cooking fires with its own average November day, from 2019 to 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s face it: The holiday season is when our ovens are working overtime.

Unfortunately, it’s also the prime time for an oven fire.

Recent findings suggest that moneyGeek recently analyzed seven years of fire department reports to the National Fire Incident Reporting System and compared each state's Thanksgiving Day cooking fires with its own average November day, from 2019 to 2025. Nationally, departments reported 3.72 times as many residential cooking fires on Thanksgiving.

And it's not just the turkey that could get ruined.

While a professional kitchen remodel averages $26,994, depending on the scope of the project and the location, according to Angi.com, fire damage might amp up that pricetag depending on whether cabinets, drywall, appliances, or partial finishes need to be removed and replaced.

Major structural damage can reach $100,000 if flames or water damaged wiring and plumbing or if the fire spread to adjacent rooms.

This is why experts recommend tried and true precautions homeowners can take to keep their home safe.

In the days leading up to the holidays, be sure to inspect the inside of your oven.

“Look specifically for older grease buildups,” says Steve Lockwood, owner of Mountain State Fire Protection, a fire safety equipment inspector and installer in Mesa, AZ.

“Over time, those can build up, become extremely hot, and they could ignite pretty easily.”.

If you’re someone who routinely stores items in your oven, be sure to empty the space entirely—before you preheat it.

“Often people don’t realize they have plastic cutting boards and casserole dishes with plastic lids stored in their oven,” Sam Taylor, disaster public affairs program manager with the American Red Cross, tells Realtor.com.

“You don’t want to run the risk of melting those items in the oven.”.

During the entire time you’re cooking a dish on your burners, stow all combustible materials away.

“Pay special attention to such items as plastic spatulas and utensils that can melt and catch fire, as well as wooden spoons, oven mitts, and paper products,” Taylor says.

Always make sure you’re not cooking foods on too-high temperatures, which can result in a fire; avoid dangerous bump-ins; and make sure pan handles don’t hang over the edge of the burners.

“This can cause the contents to spill and could cause burns or fire,” Lockwood says. And never wear a shirt with long, loose sleeves while you’re cooking.

It has been revealed that “If you’re working over an open flame, that sleeve can catch fire,” notes Taylor. “I always recommend wearing a different top that doesn’t have any fabric hanging near a flame.”.

Whatever you do, never leave the house when your oven is on, Lockwood says.

“Where most people go wrong is walking away from the kitchen,” he states. Instead, keep an eye on your oven at all times. Tip: If you have a newer digital stove, pay special attention.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot of these burners can be accidentally turned on just by leaning over them,” Lockwood states. “That’s why it’s a good practice to put the stove into a lockout mode to avoid an accidental turn on.”.

Should a fire happen, keep the oven door closed, turn off the heat, reach for your kitchen extinguisher, and alert the authorities.

Sources indicate that “Opening the oven door feeds the fire with oxygen,” Lockwood says. “In addition, while baking soda will work in a pinch, never use water on a grease fire.”.

And, if a pot on your burner catches fire, turn off the heat and put a lid or baking sheet on it immediately to smother the fire, he adds.

A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • It has been revealed that the research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
  • But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

It has been revealed that the research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

It has been revealed that treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an crucial part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

It has been revealed that if, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s crucial this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

In a recent development, the newly introduced review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

Recent findings suggest that this means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is notable given the average time people take them is much longer.

Industry observers note that importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

Sources indicate that people respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

According to recent reports, for someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

According to recent reports, continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Sources indicate that ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has introduced a new online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

It has been revealed that the IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

Sources indicate that payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

According to recent reports, for now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow users to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS said, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

The administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires users to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer plans at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have remarked they hope to pass newly introduced legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and vital pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially crucial piece in a complex puzzle.

Sources indicate that research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.

Sources indicate that when we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

In a recent development, think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

According to recent reports, changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.

Sources indicate that at the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.

In a recent development, we are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation problems, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an vital step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

Mortgage applications increased last week, despite high interest rates, inflation concerns, and a wobbly stock market.

For the week ending Nov. 20, the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—increased 6.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, increased 5% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment, though purchase applications are down 16% from a year ago.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances jumped to 7.38% this week, an increase from last week's rate of 7.31%, according to MBA calculations, and it's the highest level in five weeks.

A separate survey from Freddie Mac revealed mortgage rates rose to 7.28%, up from  7.11% last week. A year ago at this time, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.26%.

"While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist.

“Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace," he added.

Kan also noted that the share of borrowers relying on riskier adjustable-rate mortgage loans jumped to 11.5%—its highest level in more than a year.

"At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week," he stated.

Sources indicate that the share of FHA loan applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the prior week. The VA share of total applications decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5%.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% from 41.1% the previous week, but was 51% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked in to their lower interest rates.

Industry observers note that "Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%," Kan said. The latest mortgage application data comes following a week of stock market volatility. On Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly plunged into correction territory, defined as a 10% decline from their last peak.

The sell-off, driven by a wipeout in tech and AI stocks, came a day after Anthropic raised a staggering $81.34 billion during its IPO on Thursday, lifting the tech giant's valuation to $1.414 trillion.Adding to the economic stress was an announcement on Wednesday from President Donald Trump that he's proposed fresh tariffs of up to 20% on China, the EU, and a dozen other major U.S. trading partners to take effect next year.

In a recent development, mortgage rates are calculated based on several economic factors, while your loan term and credit score also influence the mortgage rate you qualify for. On the economic side, rates tend to track the 10-year Treasury note, since most 30-year mortgages are paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

In a recent development, long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. released today with $100 million in funding.

The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The company’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

It has been revealed that epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.

In a recent development, after the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

Industry observers note that the Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the manufacturer, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.

According to Epochal, its service mitigates the issue by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a manufacturer is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

It has been revealed that the Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal intends to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the fresh year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in plans to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

In a recent development, specifically, the agency said it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the initiative’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

The executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but remarked the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

Industry observers note that those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

Recent findings suggest that “While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”.

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale Fresh Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

Industry observers note that the academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

It has been revealed that the broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

In a recent development, with the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

Industry observers note that in the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in Latest York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

According to recent reports, in the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

In a recent development, the marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

It has been revealed that the broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:.

Sources indicate that in the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

In a recent development, vitalik Buterin is taking Ethereum’s decentralization philosophy down to the silicon level. The Ethereum co-founder published a deep dive into open-source chip design today, covering everything from transistor architecture and manufacturing to hardware security. His central argument? It could have implications far beyond Ethereum, and computing hardware shouldn’t remain a proprietary black box.

Recent findings suggest that could Ethereum eventually move beyond blockchain infrastructure and build its own hardware ecosystem? Vitalik’s latest exploration makes that prospect an interesting thought experiment, particularly as Nvidia dominates the computing industry.

In a recent development, vitalik’s argument starts with a familiar problem in crypto: trust. Software can be audited, code can be published, and blockchain transactions can be independently verified. Hardware, however, remains considerably harder to inspect.

A chip can contain hidden vulnerabilities or malicious modifications that consumers cannot easily detect. Even a secure wallet application cannot guarantee safety if the hardware underneath it has been compromised. This has happened recently with Ledger, and Ledger is not the only one, with Trezor and other hardware wallets being recently compromised.

“Not your silicon, not your keys.” – Vitalik put the problem bluntly.

Industry observers note that the phrase extends crypto’s self-custody mantra into the physical computing layer. Owning private keys might not mean much if users cannot trust the hardware handling them.

This is why Vitalik argues that “the hardware layer must be open for participation and tinkering too.” He wants hardware designs to become accessible to developers, researchers, and independent auditors, allowing them to examine and modify components rather than blindly trusting manufacturers.

Industry observers note that this could eventually create opportunities for Ethereum hardware focused on security, cryptographic computing, and decentralized infrastructure. Ethereum validators, hardware wallets, and zero-knowledge proof systems all depend on computing components that users need to trust.

In a recent development, nvidia built its dominance by turning GPUs into the backbone of artificial intelligence. Its hardware, software ecosystem, and CUDA platform have made competition increasingly difficult.

But Vitalik’s vision displays a different approach. Instead of chasing the fastest processors, Ethereum hardware could prioritize openness, verifiability, and security.

Vitalik acknowledges that open-source hardware faces performance limitations. Advanced chip manufacturing remains expensive and tightly controlled, leaving open designs behind the industry’s most sophisticated commercial processors.

Yet that trade-off might not matter for every workload. Vitalik writes that “Secure hardware may be 10x less efficient or more” while still being sufficient for many computing needs. That’s a striking contrast to an industry obsessed with squeezing more performance from increasingly expensive chips.

Specialized silicon designed for cryptographic operations, privacy-preserving computing, secure data processing, or decentralized networks could benefit from open designs. Developers could modify the architecture, researchers could inspect the circuitry, and manufacturers could compete to produce chips from publicly available specifications.

It has been revealed that ethereum already has an extensive developer community experimenting with cryptography and distributed computing. Extending that culture into silicon could give the ecosystem a foothold in hardware without immediately challenging Nvidia’s AI infrastructure.

The ambition could be less about building another GPU giant and more about creating a competing hardware philosophy.

Vitalik’s argument reaches beyond blockchain. He sees open hardware as a broader computing movement, where users can inspect, verify, and modify the machines they depend on.

According to recent reports, that could eventually extend into personal computers, servers, IoT devices, and secure computing infrastructure. Hardware designed around transparency could become valuable as AI, financial services, and sensitive personal data move into increasingly powerful machines.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s dominance isn’t going to disappear overnight. But Ethereum has never needed to follow the traditional technology industry’s playbook.

Its greatest strength has been building infrastructure around open participation rather than centralized ownership. If that philosophy eventually reaches the silicon powering modern computing, Ethereum could find itself competing in an industry few would have expected.

Vitalik’s latest deep dive into chip design raises a question: What happens when crypto’s decentralization movement stops at software and starts building the hardware, too?

#225479. Powerful fresh weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Powerful fresh weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle.
  • The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total.
  • Industry observers note that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

Industry observers note that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also showed reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

In a recent development, findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that "The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function.".

Sources indicate that philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential Upcoming Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis.

According to recent reports, painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

Sources indicate that weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

Industry observers note that retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

It has been revealed that while those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

According to recent reports, "Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer said. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.".

Why Diet and Exercise Still Matter.

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

According to recent reports, improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

Maintaining muscle strength is particularly important for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

According to recent reports, for individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several important questions remain unanswered.

One of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

According to recent reports, "These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer noted. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.".

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief.

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

According to recent reports, during study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity.".
