Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Half of voters stated they are paying more this year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, according to a new national poll.

Lake Research Partners and Bellwether Research & Consulting surveyed 1,000 voters between Oct. 20 and Oct. 28 on behalf of the National Health Council, and 50% noted their premiums and out-of-pocket costs are higher this year compared to last year. Among those with commercial insurance, 63% said their premiums have risen, and 60% said their out-of-pocket costs have grown year-over-year.

In addition, 25% of those surveyed said they had a claim for a prescription denied, and 24% said they waited more than two weeks for a prior authorization decision. Twenty-one percent said that they struggled to find a specialist.

In a recent development, healthcare costs and the broader economy were major factors in Democrats' significant victories in the latest midterm election. And the NHC poll finds that voters expect Congress to act on addressing the costs that they face.

Most of the surveyed voters (78%) said they believe that the healthcare system warrants major changes or a complete overhaul, and 84% said they would support a candidate that would make it a priority to reform the healthcare insurance system.

However, 74% of those surveyed rated the effort from elected officials to address affordability and access as either fair or poor.

“Holding onto a plan isn’t the same as being protected by it. Patients are watching their costs rise and their coverage change, and they’re worried about what that means for their families down the road,” stated Randall Rutta, CEO of the National Health Council, in an announcement. “The new Congress has a real opportunity to change that, and patients across the country will be watching.”.

Recent findings suggest that the survey highlights a number of potential policies that would have broad voter support. For example, 91% of those surveyed said they would support eliminating surprise medical bills and policies to require price transparency.

In addition, 90% said they would back efforts to reduce out-of-pocket costs, while 89% said they favor requiring health prepares to cover treatments that were prescribed by doctors. Eighty-eight percent support efforts to increase screening and early detection for medical risks.

"Voters aren't asking lawmakers to talk about health care differently," noted Christine Matthews, president of Bellwether Research and Consulting, in the release. "They want to see it work differently. Reform is a priority they expect the new Congress to deliver on.".

Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The number of regions where patients have limited choices for Affordable Care Act intends is on the rise, according to a latest analysis.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation report found that for the 2027 blueprint year, there are more than 200 counties in which there is only one insurer available, and close to 1,000 where there are just two aims available for consumers to choose from.

This makes for an increase of 50% from the 2026 blueprint year, with more than a third of counties having limited options on the ACA's marketplaces for 2027.

Most states (39) will have at least one county where proposal choices are limited for enrollees. For about half of these states, this is the norm and aligns with 2026, but for the rest, this marks a significant shift, the RWJF researchers wrote in the report.

Sources indicate that "For the individual market as a whole, the decline in participation is sobering but not a fatal blow," per the report. "The presence of federal and some state subsidies provides an important backstop that will likely prevent a complete meltdown.".

"Yet the prospect of a growing number of counties with little insurer participation is grim, and likely will not bode well for premium increases, morbidity or enrollment going forward," according to the report.

According to recent reports, the foundation cites a recent analysis from Wakely that found the individual market declined by 16% in the first six months of 2026. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits, cost pressures and growing administrative burdens are likely to contribute to worsening trends in this space.

It has been revealed that for instance, ACA marketplace exits from Cigna, CareSource and Medica are having a significant impact in Iowa and Indiana for the coming plan year, the researchers found. In the latter case, most Indiana counties have two or fewer plan choices.

According to recent reports, however, there are some bright spots, RWJF researchers wrote. There are certain insurers participating in the exchanges who have beefed up their footprints, and there is a smattering of new entrants. Oscar Health, for example, is planning the largest growth, entering a new state and adding new counties in some of the states it already serves.

Some insurers, like Centene and UnitedHealthcare, are making strategic exits in some markets while entering others, for a neutral impact on their footprints overall.

Insurers like Antidote Health and Peak Health are also entering newly introduced regions—even if on a limited basis in some cases—which can help staunch the bleeding.

Blue Cross Blue Shield looks also often play a key role in limited markets, as in close to 80% of counties with a single insurer, that payer is a Blues blueprint. In addition, in 12% of counties, the single insurer is Elevance Health, which operates plans as Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield.

Sources indicate that "This suggests that were it not for the somewhat unique role of Blues aims as a backstop, the threat of a bare county might be higher," per the report. "Single-state Blues, in particular, are under social and political pressure to participate in much if not all of their state, and do not feel as free to exit unprofitable counties as are publicly traded insurers.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that newly introduced -home sales surged in October as prices dropped, according to the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

Sales of upcoming single-family homes hit 701,000 in October, 14.2% above what they were in September and 7.5% above October 2025. Meanwhile, the median sales price hit $391,300, 0.3% below September 2026 and 3.2% below October 2025.

In a recent development, that was driven entirely by a surge in the South, which saw a 36.2% increase from last month and a 24.7% increase from October 2025. Northeast sales plummeted 40.0% month over month and 63.4% year over year, and the Midwest and West also saw declines.

This comes after new-home sales fell 0.6% month over month, 5.3% year over year in September, to 676,000. New-home sales were running 2.9% below 2025 numbers, Realtor.com® economists found. The median sales price in September for new homes fell 3.9% year over year to $400,400.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner noted that new home sales are still 3% below where they were in the first 10 months of 2025. And housing inventory remains low.

"Builders are lowering prices to meet demand, and the median newly introduced home sales price remains well below the median existing home sales price," Berner stated.

The National Association of Home Builders found that newly introduced homes are nearly $40,000 less expensive than existing homes. Single-family housing starts rose 4% last month amid an uneven year. The latest Realtor.com quarterly construction insights report highlights that prices on new homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue. This week, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low.

The tough environment has forced builders to get creative.

"Builders are exercising caution, preferring to line up a buyer for their homes before starting work on them rather than building as many spec homes," Berner said. "New construction remains a strong alternative to the existing home segment, offering savings on mortgage rates, sale prices, and total cost of ownership.".

Sources indicate that simon Boag, CEO of Aro Homes, says his firm opted for across-the-board price cuts on its prefabricated homes, slashing about $12 million off the asking price of its overall housing stock. It ended up holding an auction to sell a batch of 10 homes, which seems to have worked. About eight of the homes found buyers.

It has been revealed that boag tells Realtor.com that he looks at past recessions when many buyers remained in the market, even if they weren't looking aggressively. Homebuilders have to accept lower margins, but there are buyers looking for homes.

"You look at a decent homebuilder margin in the 20% range, but at 17%, you're still a viable entity," Boag says. "The business model is about, 'OK markets move all the time,' and how do you deal with that.".

Recent findings suggest that for buyers, the market may have a higher barrier to entry in the high interest rate environment. That means preparation is essential.

Earlier this week, the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index showed home values fell for the 16th straight month.

Jeffrey Ruben, president of home lending at WSFS Bank, expects the "tug of war" between high mortgage rates and affordability constraints limiting buyers in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that "While this is a good sign for home builders, it doesn't indicate what the market shows as a whole," Ruben remarked. "We are seeing the data signal movement toward a buyer's market. This is seen more clearly through existing home sales with time on market, overall sales, and total inventory.".

He noted buyers should be looking beyond standard resale listings and comparing the total monthly payment structure across both upcoming and existing homes.

"Connecting with a lender early to evaluate builder incentives alongside traditional financing options can help buyers identify opportunities in the current market without stretching their household budget," he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Researchers at the University of Cambridge are working with The Queen's Reading Room, a charity established by Her Majesty The Queen, to raise awareness of these benefits across all age groups.
  • Industry observers note that cambridge psychiatry researchers Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, reading for enjoyment may offer far more than entertainment. Whether someone prefers a classic Jane Austen novel or a Heartstopper graphic novel, research suggests that reading for pleasure is associated with better mental health, stronger empathy, and a lower risk of dementia.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge are working with The Queen's Reading Room, a charity established by Her Majesty The Queen, to raise awareness of these benefits across all age groups. Their collaboration is part of the National Year of Reading, an initiative encouraging more people to make reading part of their lives.

Industry observers note that cambridge psychiatry researchers Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr. Christelle Langley began exploring the subject while writing their 2025 book, Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. They discovered that reading for enjoyment was connected to a remarkably wide range of positive outcomes, yet the amount of research specifically examining these benefits was surprisingly limited.

In a review published in Psychological Medicine, Sahakian and Langley joined Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, to examine the available evidence. Their findings suggest that the format and type of reading matter less than the enjoyment people get from it. They also highlight how reading together, whether through book clubs or parents sharing stories with children, can provide additional benefits.

In a recent development, professor Sahakian remarked: "Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop key cognitive skills and boost our well-being. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age.".

Reading Early in Life Is Linked to Better Brain Development.

It has been revealed that despite the growing evidence of its advantages, reading for enjoyment has become less common among young people. Surveys indicate that reading rates among children and teenagers have fallen to their lowest recorded levels, with particularly steep challenges among teenage boys and children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

It has been revealed that even children who are least enthusiastic about reading recognize that it can help them academically. Nearly half acknowledge that books and other reading materials can introduce them to unfamiliar words or teach them something new.

One of the most compelling studies examined more than 10,000 young people. Conducted by Sahakian, Langley, and their colleagues, the research found that children who started reading for pleasure at an early age tended to perform better in several important areas. These included attention, memory, and executive functioning, the mental abilities involved in planning, decision-making, and managing behavior.

Industry observers note that early readers also highlighted stronger academic performance, experienced fewer mental health problems, and were more likely to develop healthier daily routines. In particular, they tended to get more sleep and spend less time using screens.

Sources indicate that dr. Langley mentioned: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading. The important thing is to find something they'd really enjoy reading about - it might be a TV program or a game - and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.".

The academic advantages may extend beyond language and literacy. Studies have also connected reading with stronger mathematical performance. Researchers suggest this relationship may arise because both activities rely on some of the same mental abilities, including language processing, memory, and executive function.

Just Five Minutes of Reading May Reduce Stress.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits of reading do not disappear after childhood. Among adults, surveys have associated reading for enjoyment with improved emotional well-being, greater relaxation, and reduced stress. Readers also tend to report more empathy, a deeper understanding of other people, and greater openness to viewpoints different from their own.

Industry observers note that for many people, books are an especially appealing way to unwind. Reading ranks as the most popular approach to stress relief, with nearly two in five adults (38%) identifying it as their preferred way to relax.

A neuroscience study commissioned by The Queen's Reading Room in 2024 found that spending just five minutes reading fiction could lower stress by as much as 20%. The study also reported improvements in concentration and problem-solving abilities, along with a reduced sense of loneliness.

Recent findings suggest that books may even provide more comfort than some traditional relaxation habits. In one survey, more respondents noted they turned to reading (35%) for comfort than to drinking wine (31%) or taking a hot bath (10%).

Reading Linked to Lower Dementia and Alzheimer's Risk.

Sources indicate that as people get older, the potential advantages of reading may become especially meaningful. Research has associated mentally stimulating leisure activities, including reading, with slower cognitive decline and a reduced likelihood of developing dementia.

One study followed nearly 5,500 adults aged 55 and older for five years. Participants who regularly took part in activities such as reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment during the study period.

Another investigation reported an even more striking association. People who read newspapers, magazines, and books had a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest that keeping the mind engaged through reading may support cognitive health in later life. However, the researchers emphasize that most of the available studies identify associations rather than proving that reading itself prevents dementia.

How Reading May Change the Structure of the Brain.

Sources indicate that what could explain the many benefits associated with reading? Brain imaging research offers some intriguing clues.

Recent findings suggest that studies have identified differences in brain structure associated with reading, particularly in regions responsible for language, learning, emotional regulation, and executive control. These differences include greater brain volume and larger cortical areas in certain regions, as well as thicker cortex in areas important for language processing.

Researchers have also observed stronger connections within the brain's white matter, which helps different regions communicate and supports the processing of language.

Although much of this evidence is correlational, some research suggests that reading-related training can directly influence the brain's physical structure.

In one small study involving 11 children with dyslexia between the ages of 7 and 11, researchers tested an eight-week training program designed to strengthen reading abilities. The exercises involved mental imagery, articulation, and tracing letters, combinations of letters, and words.

Sources indicate that following the program, the children demonstrated significant improvements in reading skills. Brain scans also revealed increases in gray matter volume in key regions, providing evidence that reading interventions can be accompanied by measurable structural changes in the brain.

Why Reading Together May Offer Even Greater Benefits.

Sources indicate that reading does not have to be a solitary activity. Researchers suggest that sharing books with other people can add a valuable social dimension, creating opportunities for connection and potentially improving both mental and physical well-being.

Sources indicate that the Queen's Reading Room has made this idea a central part of its mission. Launched on social media in January 2021, the initiative originally provided a way for people to exchange book recommendations and stay connected during pandemic lockdowns.

In a recent development, it has since expanded into an international community reaching more than 12 million people across 184 countries. Through its flagship festival, neuroscience research, and other programs, the charity works to make reading a more prominent part of everyday life.

Its activities also extend to homeless shelters and domestic violence refuges, where shared reading is used as a therapeutic resource to help people during recovery.

The social connections created through reading groups may be particularly valuable for older adults, who can face increased isolation and reduced opportunities to participate in physically demanding activities.

Recent findings suggest that professor Sahakian said: "Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia.

"While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may not be so mobile - they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy.".

The researchers' overall message is that people can benefit from reading at any stage of life. Whether someone enjoys novels, newspapers, comics, or stories shared with friends, making time for reading may help support cognitive health, emotional well-being, and social connection.

Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, added: "At The Queen's Reading Room, we have seen first-hand the transformative power of individual and shared reading to change lives. Books truly do make life better, and we're excited to do our bit to help everyone, everywhere, make more room for reading.".

UPDATED 20:41 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Employees working at frontier artificial intelligence model companies Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC have been butting heads with executives over advanced models whose reasoning is such that the models pose to danger to humanity, according to a report by Axios today based on more than two dozen sources familiar with the current standoff at the companies.

The report states the models in question are far more powerful than anything that has so far reached the public, showing great leaps forward in reasoning in many areas that have been difficult, “if not impossible,” to control during tests. It appears that some staff err on the side of caution and believe the training should stop completely while others believe they can be reined in.

Recent findings suggest that “If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us… they will in fact be able to trick us successfully,” one of the researchers told Axios. “And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.”.

According to recent reports, after Open AI’s AI agents seemingly went berserk earlier this year and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc., there have been calls to pause AI development until safety can be assured. The state of California this month rolled out a lawsuit calling Open AI a “public nuisance,” whose models currently pose cybersecurity risks while threatening the “well-being of society.”.

The debate on how far we should go before we step on the brakes has largely been overshadowed by companies, and the countries where they are developed, steaming ahead winning the AI race. In the Axios report, many of the anonymous claimed executives are “out of touch” with safety issues as they put profit first.

Nonetheless, Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei has been vocal about the “existential risks to humanity” that AI might bring. In his recent essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei remarked “pacing” is notable, warning that authoritarian regimes such as China must agree to cooperate in moving forward slowly with the frontier models. President Trump has been less than supportive of such measures, calling the threats to humanity a “hoax.”.

#225469. Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field.
  • An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss.
  • Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago.

Industry observers note that the investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered latest genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.

In a recent development, the study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

It has been revealed that at first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.".

How the Upcoming Eye Disease Affects Night Vision.

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

It has been revealed that however, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

Sources indicate that "We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.".

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss.

An key question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Recent findings suggest that researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

Sources indicate that beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

It has been revealed that "Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.".

By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

In an interview with Fierce Healthcare, he mentioned that the upcoming role comes at "an exciting time" to be a part of a strategy like Surest.

It has been revealed that under the model, Surest eliminates deductibles for a copayment-only approach, where members' costs are tied to the quality and value for their provider. Members connect to the Surest app or website to compare the cost between different providers.

"Affordability is a challenge every year, but especially right now, for employers," Clark remarked. "We've seen demand for Surest and other sort of alternative health looks just skyrocket over the last year. And being part of being able to deliver that and offer solutions to employers is incredibly exciting.".

Industry observers note that unitedHealthcare first rolled out the unit in 2016 as Bind before rebranding as Surest in 2022 with an eye on growth. In a 2023 report, the tech giant said that Surest members had 6% fewer emergency department visits and 13% fewer inpatient admissions compared to people enrolled in traditional commercial aims at the same company.

The proposal also saw a 20% increase in visits to a physician and 9% increase in preventative physical exams compared to the members in traditional intends.

Industry observers note that in a 2024 analysis, conducted by Aon, the tech giant found that Surest enrollees generated $400 or more in cost claims savings per year. That study also identified improvements around spending and utilization across all age groups and accounting for several conditions.

Industry observers note that clark said that in a traditional health proposal, only about 15% of people hit their deductible for the year, meaning they're ultimately not using their insurance during that time frame. Surest removes that problem by eliminating the deductible and puts the power in the consumers' hands to make choices for their own care.

It has been revealed that he added that the Net Promoter Score for Surest is higher than its other commercial plan offerings. Consumers report satisfaction with the digital experience and the cost certainty that the plan presents, Clark mentioned.

"It's very much like the Amazon shopping experience, but for healthcare, which hasn't happened before," Clark mentioned.

Surest also aims to personalize the member experience by leaning on AI and other digital tools to present data on providers and costs that may be of use to the user, while leaving the ultimate decision in their hands.

It has been revealed that "The consumer is in charge with their doctor in making those decisions," Clark said. "But we want to make sure that we are giving you, similar to what you would see with any shopping app, a personalized recommendation of what is a good fit.".

Clark remarked that starting his career on the actuarial side of healthcare made plain how much of a challenge affordability can be, and that drew him to pursue his current path. Prior to UnitedHealthcare, he served as an associate partner at McKinsey and as an actuary at Cigna.

Through Surest, he believes he can help lead the charge toward a more modern healthcare system, he said.

In a recent development, as for the future of Surest, the first piece is continuing to make sure the team delivers on a personalized and simple-to-understand experience for consumers. The next level is building on that consumer-focused experience to add a provider layer, and work with them on the quality and value scores that are surfaced to members.

Sources indicate that for example, a provider may consistently recommend a patient seek an MRI scan at a hospital rather than at a lower-cost lab. And Surest is gaining the "critical mass" of members where providers actively want to have these conversations, Clark noted.

"I see that as sort of the next evolution beyond working with consumers and members: moving to providers as well," he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades—and causing a time honored tradition to be postponed for the first time in its history.
  • Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are stated to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.
  • The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades—and causing a time honored tradition to be postponed for the first time in its history.

Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are stated to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.

The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.

While flooding is a major consideration, meteorologists are more concerned about the powerful winds accompanying the storm, which could result in tree damage, power outages, and other disasters for homeowners to contend with on the big day.

Industry observers note that the high winds ultimately forced the hands of Newly introduced York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's, who late on Wednesday confirmed that the parade would be pushed off until the following Saturday Nov. 28, due to the weather.

The storm will ramp up in the Southeast on Wednesday, according to The Weather Channel, with rain, wind, and coastal flooding causing hazardous conditions for travelers heading home for the holiday.

Because temperatures have dropped as well, snow is also likely in parts of Missouri and Illinois beginning later in the day, continuing into the night, into Thanksgiving.

By Thanksgiving Thursday, the storm will have made its way north into the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, before steadily moving into Newly introduced England by afternoon or evening.

While wind is top of mind given the milestone parade, significant coastal flooding along the East Coast is poised to cause beach erosion, flooded coastal streets, and potential structural damage.

Moderate to major flooding is possible from Georgia to Long Island, alongside at least minor flooding in Upcoming England, with any heavy rain during high tide worsening the inundation, notes Weather.com.

Peak water levels will hit Georgia and South Carolina on Wednesday morning, before shifting north to North Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, the Jersey Shore, and Long Island on Thanksgiving morning, and reaching coastal New England by Thursday and Friday midday.

Conditions could be especially severe in the mid-Atlantic, with widespread road flooding expected across Jersey Shore communities such as Atlantic City and Ocean City, water levels in Cape May and coastal Delaware potentially hitting their highest mark since January 2016, and Ocean City, MD, approaching its 1998 all-time record.

As the storm threatened to ground the balloons and drench the anticipated thousands of spectators, local outlets reported early Wednesday that Mayor Mamdani, the police commissioner and Macy's executives will announce the postponement of the Thanksgiving parade late on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that the parade was scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST on Thursday, on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, and the National Weather Service had already issued a high wind warning before the call was made to move the parade.

The last reports predict that wind gusts will already exceed limits before the parade is even set to start.

"There is a significant risk that gusty winds ahead of the nor’easter cause the parade balloons to at least be lower than usual, and it’s possible they are not able to fly at all," AccuWeather Vice President of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin remarked ahead of the announcement .

According to recent reports, "This scenario is most likely should the storm move a bit more quickly up the coast. If it’s slower, the wind may intensify after the parade is over.".

Sustained winds must remain below 23 mph and gusts have to be lower than 34 mph for the balloons to fly.

The last balloon grounding was in 1971, but the parade has never been canceled due to weather in its 100-year history.

Power outages and tree damage are possible, according to the Weather Prediction Center, as wind gusts of 50-plus mph are forecasted along the coast with 40-plus mph gusts inland into the Interstate-95 corridor through at least Friday.

As of Monday evening, the National Weather Service warned that “tree damage and power outages will be possible” from the storm on Thanksgiving Day.

It has been revealed that the forecasts put the strongest gusts along the mid-Atlantic coast and inland corridors on Thursday. Along the Newly introduced Jersey shore and Delaware beaches, gusts will reach 50 to 60 mph—with 40 to 50 mph inland—prompting NWS Mount Holly to issue a high wind watch for the coastal strip from late Wednesday night through late Thursday night.

In a recent development, farther south, Southeast Virginia and Northeast North Carolina face 2 to 3 inches of rain alongside east to northeast gusts of 40 to 50 mph inland and potentially 50 to 60 mph on the coast, where NWS Wakefield noted a high wind watch may be needed. Meanwhile, Washington, DC, Baltimore, and Northern Virginia can expect 1 to 3 inches of rain and Thanksgiving Day gusts of 35 to 50 mph, which NWS Sterling warned could be “strong to perhaps damaging.”.

Recent findings suggest that the threat shifts northward later in the day, with Southern New England forecast to see gusts of 40 to 55 mph and up to 60 mph on Cape Cod and the islands. According to NWS Boston, the strongest winds in that region will arrive on Thursday night. In Rhode Island, forecasters specifically note the potential for isolated power outages late Thursday night and overnight, with coastal areas facing the highest risk.

Meanwhile, California has its own winter weather whirlwind to contend with, including massive waves battering the coastline.

According to the NWS, record-breaking king tides, combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to Southern California during this Thanksgiving week, with the greatest impacts anticipated Wednesday and Thursday, potentially flooding coastal properties and causing significant beach erosion.

“A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services mentioned on Friday.

Industry observers note that the mayor of San Francisco warned of “high tides and rain that this city has never seen before,” in the days leading up to the holiday, asking the public to avoid all but essential travel. The National Weather Service in the Bay Area added low areas would be prone to flooding, including San Francisco International Airport, which would be an added hindrance to travel to say the least.

Meanwhile, Southern California cities such as Newport Beach, Seal Beach, and Long Beach have put up miles of sand berms, some 15 feet tall or higher, to try to keep the ocean back, according to The Washington Post.

This weather seems to be a perfect storm of the warm waters of record-breaking El Niño colliding with an extra-high “king tide,” which the area already had to contend with a few weeks ago.

"In California, tides will be about half a foot higher than the highest in October," physical oceanographer Greg Dusek told Weather.com.

"This means that even if El Niño doesn't increase water levels further, there will be significant flooding along the California coast," Dusek said.

Forecasts predict the worst of the storms could strike on Tuesday and Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day.

#225464. Tech Report: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

Tech Report: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension.
  • Recent findings suggest that losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile.
  • The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Recent findings suggest that losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a fresh study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

The research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," notes Cohen. "The scope of this latest analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.".

AI Analysis Reveals New Benefits of Brown Fat.

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

The team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover important details about brown fat and its effects on health.

Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

Recent findings suggest that the analysis demonstrated that brown fat's location could be just as important as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

Recent findings suggest that "For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he claims. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers.".

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat.

As the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

To explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

Even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

Recent findings suggest that "The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," indicates Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.".

In a recent development, additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan indicated increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health.

It has been revealed that beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues," says Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

Recent findings suggest that however, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

The discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

It has been revealed that losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

"There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start.".

According to recent reports, materials provided by Rockefeller University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Industry observers note that stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 16 to 27.

Waystar noted Tuesday it will integrate its AI-driven revenue cycle solutions into Google Cloud’s recently revealed Gemini for healthcare solution.

Sources indicate that the integration reflects an expanded partnership between Waystar and Google Cloud. Through it, consumers will have increased access to Waystar AltitudeAI innovations, advanced analytics and revenue cycle insights.

“By bringing Waystar's AI-powered revenue cycle capabilities into Gemini for healthcare, we're helping providers simplify some of the most complex operational and financial tasks in care delivery,” said Aashima Gupta, Google Cloud managing director of healthcare, in a statement. “Together, we are unifying data and workflows in a secure, governed workspace that drives better outcomes across the healthcare ecosystem.”.

OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT’s health capabilities across various channels, it said Thursday.

The tech giant’s Health feature is expanding to desktop app, Androids and its personal AI agents—dubbed dots.

Among the newly introduced capabilities include:.

ChatGPT Health is currently available to Free, Go, Plus, and Pro customers in the U.S., while dots are available to Pro users.

Oracle launched a upcoming agentic experience for life science organizations to improve clinical trial operations.

Oracle Life Science AI Agents is right now available for early adopters with a focus on portfolio monitoring, trial planning and conduct. The firm looks to expand into clinical development domains, including data management, post-trial analytics and trial design.

Agents are designed to work with human oversight, executives say.

Oracle Health and Life Sciences EVP and General Manager Seema Verma noted in a statement clinical development requires companies to “coordinate complex operational activity.”.

According to recent reports, “We are bringing AI-assisted intelligence into clinical trial operations to help organizations to monitor performance, identify emerging risks, and coordinate responses across the trial lifecycle,” Verma said. “By combining Oracle’s Life Sciences applications, AI-assisted capabilities, connected data services, on a secure, scalable cloud infrastructure, we are helping organizations coordinate clinical research workflows and operational decisions across their clinical trial environments.”.

Agentic firm Artera declared the roll out of an intake solution using AI Agents to collect, check and complete information throughout the patient visit.

Sources indicate that artera Intake has three core workflows, executives say: pre-visit intake, in-office and walk-in intake and complex form and consent digitization. The workflows are housed in a new Intake Hub, according to the Nov. 19 announcement.

Chief Product and Strategy Officer Zach Wood remarked in a statement what differentiates the solution from others is “where it starts.”.

“Most intake solutions are built first, and providers have to change their workflows to fit them,” Wood noted. “We start with the provider. We learn how their teams and patients actually move through intake, then build the agentic solution around that, together.”.

Wood continued, “That starting point shapes everything that follows, and is designed to drive faster adoption, more completed intake and real value for practices.”.

Amazon Connect Health announced Nov. 17 the launch of expanded patient access capabilities through the agentic solution.

As of the date of the announcement, four new capabilities are generally available to users: appointment management, prescription management, information assistance and password reset.

The firm states the expansion builds on the foundation of Amazon Connect Health, which included patient verification, patient insights, ambient documentation and more.

It has been revealed that one health system using the tool is Philadelphia-based Temple Health. AVP of Patient Access Joseph Alfonsi said in a statement the tool has handled patient verification on thousands of calls weekly since the system went live in June.

According to recent reports, “Building on that success, we’re excited to expand agentic patient access capabilities for prescription management, portal password resets, and information assistance,” Alfonsi mentioned. “Our patients shouldn’t have to wait until business hours—or wait on hold—to manage routine tasks. Now they can verify once and take care of everyday needs in a single call, any time of day, and our team can focus on the conversations where a human touch matters most.”.

Glen came in second place in the competition dance series, with two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech taking home the coveted Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

And while the contestants share a spot on Team USA—for which they've both brought home gold medals—they promptly bonded in the competition as their professional dance partners, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach, are married.

When asked how she felt about the results after the finale, Glenn told Extra she "couldn't ask for a better result," and described a "triumphant feeling" as she walked away from Season 35 having earned 10s across the board in all three of her final performances.

According to recent reports, "From day one, we all met up, had a little dinner over at their house, and we said, 'We wanna go 1-2,'" she explained to the outlet. "And we didn't specify, like, whatever happens, happens, but the fact that we came in here and we both got those perfect scores. We both did everything we could and it was truly in the hands of the people at home. I'm really proud of what we did and I'm really, really happy that Team USA took it home.".

It has been revealed that the group—who have been unofficially dubbed "Team USA and the Pashkovs" by fans and even the official U.S. Olympic and Paralmypic team all season—have been close collaborators throughout the competition.

During the Nov. 10 episode, when teams were paired off and required to compete in two-on-two dance-offs, Glenn and Pashkov and Frech and Karagach put a friendly spin on the format by switching partners mid-choreography as they performed a Rumba to "The Boy Is Mine" by Brandy and Monica.

"It felt more like a team dance than anything else," Karagach told Us magazine. "We came together ,and we had the best time sharing the dance floor, and we couldn't also not end swapping partners because I've always wanted to dance with Amber, and Ezra and Pasha secretly wanted to dance with each other. So that was fun.".

The competitors-turned-pals took to social media to share plenty of heartwarming behind-the-scenes moments throughout the experience, providing a glimpse at what their down time is like between rehearsals. In one Sept. 18 post, Pashkov wrote, "We're a tightly-knit fam now.".

In a post-finale interview with Deadline, Glenn described the moment she had realized Frech would win. The Plano, TX native noted, "I don't know if I felt as many emotions watching a performance as I did when watching Ezra and Dani. It was like, at first, it's excitement. I'm like, 'I love that Linkin Park [song].' And then horror, fear, and like, panic.'".

In a recent development, the moment Glenn was referring to was the malfunction in which Frech's prosthetic fell off mid-performance. Frech and Karagach quickly communicated while dancing, allowing him to secure it into place properly and complete the routine.

"I think I gasped so loud I threw my rib out again," Glenn continued. "So then, the physical pain and just like, fear, panic, and then just awe, inspiration, something you feel in your core. I know that's a saying, but like you feel it in your gut, and it takes your breath away, and that's what it was.".

Glenn mentioned that in that moment, she "was like, 'They won.'" She even added that she "would feel bad" if she had taken home the trophy after seeing Frech and Karagach pull off "such a perfect dance" after "working so hard for it all season.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in a letter to tech giant employees, Ramaswami (pictured) noted he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

Industry observers note that in a letter to tech giant employees, Ramaswami (pictured) noted he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

“Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this firm and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

Ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the company delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The organization reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the manufacturer guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the company during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

In a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami noted he believes the company is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

“[We have] transformed the organization to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami stated. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

Sources indicate that according to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the new era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

Ramaswami’s departure from the company should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix confirmed it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

It has been revealed that VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the company by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

In April, Ramaswami appeared on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s mobile livestreaming studio, where he talked about how Nutanix is shifting away from HCI to focus on more of a “disaggregated infrastructure” strategy to support demand for autonomous AI agents:.

For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout.
  • In a recent development, the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues.
  • It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly notable for supporting mental well-being.

In a recent development, the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health.

It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to latest academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an crucial research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

To investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise showed the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

According to recent reports, the researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week demonstrated a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health.

In a recent development, taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

Sources indicate that however, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life.".

Recent findings suggest that "Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an crucial part of a healthy learning environment.".

Industry observers note that funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Millennials living in rural areas have 42% more documented chronic conditions on average compared to those in other environments, a new report from athenaInstitute found.

And, millennials in rural communities are 47% more likely to have at least two chronic conditions. This heavier chronic disease burden extends to other generations as well, analysts note.

Half of Baby Boomers (50.4%) in rural areas have three or more documented conditions, which the report says is “on par” with non-rural individuals in the Silent and Greatest generations.

In a recent development, the 2026 Rural Ambulatory Care Report (PDF) analyzed athenahealth network data from 12.3 million rural patients between 2021 and 2025, along with more than 30,000 clinicians and 1,861 rural practices across the U.S. It examined factors such as appointment activity, workforce composition, payments, and more.

Athenahealth CMO and athenaInstitute co-chair Nele Jessel, M.D., stated in a statement the findings show that while rural practices are not “standing still in the face of enormous challenges,” there are “limits to how much more they can absorb as patient needs continue to grow.”.

“They are adapting how they deliver care and finding ways to keep patients connected to the care they need,” Jessel remarked. “With renewed focus on rural healthcare, there is a real opportunity to build on what is working by investing in the workforce, technology and models of care that can help these practices continue serving the communities that depend on them.”.

Primary care physicians in rural areas have to wear multiple hats, as specialty care needs at practices are higher in rural communities.

The report found that primary care handles 68.7% of visits involving anxiety or depression diagnoses versus 55.1% in non-rural areas. Moreover, 25% of rural patients with documented anxiety or depression had a substance use disorder—up from 19.8% in non-rural communities.

Data highlights rural and non-rural healthcare practices collected roughly the same share of what they were owed by insurers in 2025, but analysts note a difference in patient balances.

Rural practices collected about $70 of every $100 owed, while non-rural practices collected about $78—which analysts say is about a 10% gap.

Another potential source of financial vulnerability for rural practices is Medicaid. Medicaid covered 27.5% of rural visits, which analysts note leaves these practices more exposed to eligibility changes set to begin in 2027.

The Home Audit That Could Save Homeowners Thousands—and Cost You Only $50

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that for example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home.
  • Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric tech giant—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

It has been revealed that for example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric tech giant—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

While experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture challenges.

Industry observers note that “When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold challenges that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” claims Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are vital as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien says.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” says O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting upcoming, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

It has been revealed that according to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” indicates Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, indicates that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.
