📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a latest clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," states Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have key therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone.".

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets.

Sources indicate that an estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

According to recent reports, these eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

Industry observers note that to compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss.

Sources indicate that participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating intends, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

Industry observers note that the diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

Sources indicate that by the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

Keto Diet Reduces Liver Fat by 67%.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several notable indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

In a recent development, participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

According to recent reports, the ketogenic group demonstrated the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

Sources indicate that one result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes.

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

In a recent development, these differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an key improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially notable distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful fresh obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study indicates that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits.".

In a recent development, although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful.
  • Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.
  • Recent findings suggest that A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

Recent findings suggest that A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the latest house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

Sources indicate that as you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

In a recent development, greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert states, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the newly introduced place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the fresh address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

It has been revealed that as you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the latest home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#225450. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings.
  • Recent findings suggest that as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically.
  • Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a upcoming study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, fresh research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

Recent findings suggest that as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a upcoming study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body.

The discovery raises notable questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health.

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health matter.

Industry observers note that in 2026, the federal government introduced a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the Upcoming England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

Industry observers note that however, an crucial question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The latest findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

According to recent reports, "Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," mentioned Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue.".

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

Recent findings suggest that "Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min noted.

Industry observers note that to investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

According to recent reports, hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," stated Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Industry observers note that co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

Sources indicate that "This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts.".

It has been revealed that by revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a fresh dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

#225449. Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1711 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.
  • Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.
  • It has been revealed that but the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.

Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.

It has been revealed that but the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings. Its Seller Central policy explicitly banned complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

Despite that, you’re likely to still find listings for tiny homes on the platform, which makes it even more imperative that you learn the ABCs of ADUs.

To begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure. Tiny homes are usually freestanding, compact units typically under 400 square feet—sometimes on foundations or other times on wheels like an RV.

But in both cases, the structures are economical and effective ways to achieve additional living space.

"As urban populations swell and sustainability becomes a central focus, the ability to build smaller, energy-efficient homes with reduced environmental impact will be key," indicates Paul Dashevsky, co-CEO of Maxable, a leader in ADU planning, building, and development.

But while tiny homes and ADUs may indeed be poised to make a positive impact toward solving the housing crisis, potential buyers need to know that you can't just plop one anywhere you please. Not to mention, tiny homes ordered online will probably also require hiring a contractor to help with assembly (adding to the overall cost).

With all that in mind, let's dig in to the details you must know prior to purchasing any ADU or tiny home. Because the last thing you want is to find yourself trying to return an entire house to sender.

Industry observers note that while it can be exciting to imagine buying a "house" for $10,000 online, it's very important to not just look at the photos and think that's what will arrive. Read the fine print and all the reviews.

According to recent reports, "Are you buying a complete tiny house that comes fully built, transported and rolled/craned into your backyard—or are you buying a bunch of parts that need to be assembled?" asks Dashevsy. "If assembly is required, make sure you first speak to a local contractor and determine the price of assembly.".

Though some of the advertisements—like this two-story foldable container home—say they only require five people to assemble it in 30-minutes, are you really going to feel confident asking a couple friends over—with the promise of pizza and beer afterward—to get the job done?

Sources indicate that the reality is that most people—unless they're cool with an adult-sized Lego project—will need a skilled contractor to assist with a tiny home or ADU build. Dashevsky suggests looking for a licensed general contractor with ADU experience. "You can find them through referrals or on sites like GreatBuildz, Angi, or Yelp," claims Dashevsky.

As for the cost, it varies according to the type of tiny home or ADU.

"A brand new ADU built on your site will greatly depend on your region and the size of the ADU, but a good range is $80,000 to $400,000," notes Dashevsky, though assembling a prefab ADU may run less predicated on its complexity.

Before you buy a prefab ADU or tiny home, you must make sure that the city or county you live in allows for such dwellings on your property.

Recent findings suggest that you can start by doing an Internet search for this information. Look for your city’s planning or building department. Most will have a website, and you can probably glean some information there.

However, if you're seriously in the ready-to-buy stage, it's probably wise to visit one of these offices in person for a consultation. Make sure they allow the kind of tiny home or ADU you're considering on your property. Also confirm where you’re allowed to install it. And ask about any necessary permits, building codes, and occupancy requirements in your area.

Industry observers note that "Essentially, you want to know every single guideline they have for this structure," says Dashevsky. "The last thing you want is a tiny home you have to sell or return because your city wont allow it.".

Alternatively, you can hire a local architect who is experienced in ADUs—they should know all the city/county requirements for your location.

Unless you want to live in the dark with no water, you're going to need electrical and plumbing hookups for your tiny home or ADU. But some people who purchase a dwelling online neglect to consider those details in advance.

"A tiny home won’t do you much good if it isn’t connected to electrical power, water, and sewer at the very least," notes Dashevsky.

It has been revealed that speak with your local building department or utility providers to understand the process and costs to tie your tiny house in to municipal services. Or, if you have your own water well and septic tank, ask a contractor how much it will run to connect to these facilities.

For those who don't fully understand what this entails, connecting utilities to a tiny house or ADU is very similar to that for a normal house.

It has been revealed that "You dig a trench from the location of the existing utilities—water, sewer, electrical gas—and run fresh pipes to the location of the new unit," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you—this is not a DIY project— and it will probably cost around $10,000 to $20,000.".

If your region is prone to weather events or natural disasters, you'll want to ensure that your tiny house has been tested to withstand extreme conditions.

According to recent reports, "Is it rated to withstand snow, sleet, winds, earthquakes, hurricanes?" says Dashevsky. "There is no point spending a lot of money that gets wiped out in the first rainy season.".

What exactly are you looking for when you're assessing a tiny home or ADU for purchase? Check to see if it states it's made of fire-resistant materials or has a fire rating (the best is a Class A or 1). Also see if it lists a wind rating—the Beaufort Wind Scale is most commonly used with levels ranging from 1 (light air) to 12 (hurricane winds). Finally, look for an earthquake resistance rating (0-9, like the Richter scale) or a Seismic Building Code. All of these will help give you an idea of the quality of the unit you're considering.

If you're having the ADU or tiny home built from scratch, it's a slightly different story as your contractor will be required to make sure it's up to code.

Sources indicate that "ADUs are built under the same guiding building code—International Residential Code (IRC)—as principal houses and don't have any less requirements for seismic/hurricane/snow or structural bracing," says Jeremy Tetreault, of Four Brothers Design + Build in Washington, D.C. "They are treated with the same level of scrutiny and energy ratings, too, so you should have nothing to worry about from a standpoint of being less equipped to withstand natural events.".

Getting insurance for your ADU or tiny home can sometimes be a hassle, so this is something to consider before buying an accessory unit.

Tiny homes—especially of the DIY or prefab variety—typically don't qualify for homeowners insurance policies. However, they may qualify for RV or mobile home insurance—especially if it's a tiny home on wheels (THOW)—as long as they meet building codes. The good news with this, however, is that you can often save 50% or more over regular homeowners insurance with a tiny home.

For people who have a tiny home on their property along with another home, or who build an ADU onto an existing home, it may be possible to insure the unit under the "other structures" portion of an existing homeowners policy.

The bottom line is you should speak with an insurance broker about what it will take to insure your ADU or tiny home since that will be an additional expense.

Industry observers note that it's easy to get sucked into the idea that an ADU or a tiny home you can purchase online is a great deal! But it's important to be realistic about all the additional costs. We already mentioned the possibility of needing to hire a contractor to help with construction—and maybe a plumber and an electrician to hook up the utilities. But there are some other hidden costs of which potential buyers should also be aware.

It has been revealed that to begin with, do you need to lay a foundation for your tiny home? If it's on wheels, then you can probably get away without one. But for people looking for a more permanent smaller housing situation, turning it into a tiny home on foundation (THOF) will give the structure more stability.

In a recent development, "Unless your tiny home is on wheels, it should sit on a concrete pad or foundation made of cement," states Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you but expect a ballpark cost of about $5,000 to $15,000.".

Also, if you purchase a home prebuilt but don't have room to roll it into the space where you plan to put it, you may need to pay for extra equipment. For example, if you have to "crane it in" then you need to factor in the price of hiring that service as well.

"The bottom line is that you really need to know all the costs involved, which are very likely to end up being close to double the Amazon 'price,'" says Dashevsky.

However, as long as you know what to expect, ordering up a tiny home or ADU can be a prime way to create an affordable housing solution.

Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different.
  • It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.
  • The firm said today that owners can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

It has been revealed that rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

The firm said today that owners can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant owners first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic noted people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the manufacturer said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s fresh “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

Sources indicate that in a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Sources indicate that ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq.

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026.

Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to owners, Anthropic stated.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic noted. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

It has been revealed that there is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”.

Recent findings suggest that that could be a pretty substantial downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%.

According to recent reports, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

According to recent reports, it is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the company a valuation greater than the value of every home right now listed for sale.

AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior, with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments.

Markets are presently pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," claims Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith.

Industry observers note that your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

Industry observers note that the credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease.
  • The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's.
  • "These findings break newly introduced ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward latest ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

"These findings break newly introduced ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.".

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's.

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

In a recent development, two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.

It has been revealed that microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is notable for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role.

"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," mentioned Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us latest insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.".

In a recent development, the researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

That distinction could be vital for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments.

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.".

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an key opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

Industry observers note that however, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

Sources indicate that the work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (MASSIVE Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she remarked. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration.".

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal.

Sources indicate that the research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who claims participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his aims for a career in medicine.

Sources indicate that "I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he noted. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science.".

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.

Materials provided by University of Virginia Health System. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records.

In a recent development, under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

Recent findings suggest that confirming bladder cancer right now requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

Sources indicate that to explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases.

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

In a recent development, the model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Industry observers note that importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

In a recent development, the AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

A Upcoming Approach to Early Cancer Screening.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

Industry observers note that for example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, noted: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022.".

Recent findings suggest that "Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods.".

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

It has been revealed that dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved.".

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages.".

More Research Needed Before Clinical Use.

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's crucial to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions.".

The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video firm everyone used during the pandemic.
  • Sources indicate that total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters.
  • The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 23:43 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video firm everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Sources indicate that total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and revealed its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

Industry observers note that the concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

In a recent development, nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Sources indicate that zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually remarked to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan noted. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan remarked it is nearing 2 million monthly active customers, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

Recent findings suggest that that is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

Industry observers note that A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

It has been revealed that customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang stated.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom stated at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

In a recent development, chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she stated, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a substantial winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

Industry observers note that there is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan mentioned. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another organization’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

It has been revealed that although these concerns came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of fresh products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”.

In a recent development, zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s vital to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

According to recent reports, for information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

It has been revealed that that is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their latest home in the Cotswalds, and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood, the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom.

Northwood shared a look inside the family's latest digs in a Nov. 22 Instagram post, noting that he and Markle had recently spent quite a bit of quality time together, including a lunch date and a visit to her newly introduced property.

During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood stated they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah, "who has just started weaning" and is exploring upcoming foods.

According to recent reports, "She was very excited for all the newly introduced flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment.".

Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a Newly introduced York-inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website, Northwood divulged more about their catchup.

Recent findings suggest that "I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood noted of their lunch date. "Since we last saw each other, she’s had her second baby and I’ve had my first. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world.".

Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything.".

The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet.

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail.

They first made looks to establish a private residence in the U.K. in August of this year, six years after quitting their roles as working members of the British royal family to relocate to a $14.7 million home in Montecito, CA.

Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false.".

In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family.".

In a recent development, "Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me," he stated of Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. "I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience.".

In a recent development, he also admitted that "it's nice to be back" on "U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there.".

The family looks to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas.

It has been revealed that during a Nov. 20 appearance on the British morning show, "This Morning," Harry revealed the family's prepares for Thanksgiving and Christmas, noting that mother-in-law Doria Ragland will be joining them.

"My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he remarked, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu.

The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography.

"Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People. "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.

"Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone," the source added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by Upcoming York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

In a recent development, after 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

According to recent reports, “They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”.

According to recent reports, in addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it indicates ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

After the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

According to recent reports, “Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you strategy your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”.

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

Industry observers note that the property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt remarked. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only highlighted it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” stated Chesnutt.

According to recent reports, after over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The fresh owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” mentioned Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”.

It has been revealed that chesnutt could not disclose whether the the latest owners proposal to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

Recent findings suggest that “It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” mentioned Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that owners will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

Recent findings suggest that when writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Sources indicate that storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

It has been revealed that in the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

In a recent development, social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

Recent findings suggest that to encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt people to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

💡 Key Takeaways
