  • Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set.
  • Curve also figures in how Sequent got started.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today confirmed that it has raised $2.2 million in latest funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

It has been revealed that following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who mentioned AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

Sources indicate that for now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor aims priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

In a recent development, frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.
  • In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T.
  • The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.

In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.

Recent findings suggest that despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision.

The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote, with only Arpit Gupta, an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams, voting no.

According to recent reports, but it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze.

Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes.

Industry observers note that operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially.

“Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, mentioned in June.

Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the Newly introduced York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid.".

The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in many cases, a health diagnosis can be life-changing. From dealing with symptoms to navigating treatment, managing medical issues is no easy feat.

And while accessibility upgrades and wellness integrations can certainly make a home more habitable in these instances, some people choose to pack up and move altogether—particularly celebrities.

Because their diagnoses may be complicated by the nuances that come along with fame and being in the public eye, it’s no surprise that some celebs may choose to find a home with more privacy when faced with health challenges.

Of course, celebrities may also have the means to relocate when particular symptoms could be managed more easily in a different climate.

Although some high profile individuals prefer to keep these kinds of decisions close to the chest, a handful of celebs have spoken candidly about the health-related circumstances that inspired them to migrate.

Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg recently offloaded their longtime Illinois residence for $2.6 million. The transaction comes just as “The Masked Singer” host has publicly shared her experience dealing with the effects of “mold and mycotoxin poisoning.”.

According to recent reports, during the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed that she’s been living in a tent after undergoing the costly experience of remediating her home.

In a later episode, McCarthy also noted that she has discarded all of her clothing and furniture in a continued attempt to escape the mold.

In the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I’m so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” McCarthy mentioned.

McCarthy and Wahlberg have yet to make a permanent move, but the sale of their St. Charles property could certainly be the first step towards change.

Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday and his wife, Leslie Holliday, were left with no choice but to leave the dream home they’d built in Stillwater, OK, when he was diagnosed with a respiratory disease.

“The doctor stated he needed to get to dry climate quick,” listing agent Vincent Clark told the Phoenix Business Journal.

Clark is the agent representing the sale of the Paradise Valley, AZ property the Hollidays initially relocated to.

They purchased the $10.6 million home in February of this year after the World Series champion received the diagnosis a week after a water leak had affected their 136-acre custom home in Oklahoma, which is still on the market for $8.95 million.

While the sprawling Arizona property was well-equipped with “substantial healthy-home enhancements” including air and water filtration and conditioning systems, Clark revealed that the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guest house, although the 7,781-square-foot home they’re hoping to sell includes transferred approved plans for an 845-square-foot guest casita.

In an Aug.10 social media post, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” alum Mikayla Matthews admitted that her “home situation is always up in the air.”.

The reality TV personality was diagnosed with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS), which she believes was triggered by extended exposure to mold-related toxins.

She and her family spent much of 2026 traveling in hopes of easing her symptoms, and temporarily relocated to Hawaii in May before heading to Florida in June in pursuit of a humid climate.

“The heavy metals in the air from Great Salt Lake drying up add to my toxic load everyday, so I can’t detox everything out,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

In October, Matthews revealed that her family was leaving the home she says was “making” her “sick,” and had purchased a new home in Utah, which is still under construction.

Bella Hadid recently purchased an idyllic $5.5 million home in Colorado, but it’s not the first time she’s snapped up a property with a stunning connection to nature.

In 2024, the model spoke to Allure about her decision to take a break from the industry in pursuit of a more laid back lifestyle in Fort Worth, TX, citing mental health struggles including severe anxiety and brain fog, as well as her longtime battle with Lyme disease.

The move marked a focus on her mental and physical health, as well as a dedication to a passion she’d lost with fame: horseback riding.

At the time, Hadid was dating Adan Banuelos, an equestrian trainer. The pair were seemingly on and off for two years before separating earlier in 2026, but during their time together, she began competing in amateur cutting horse competitions after a history as a longtime show jumper.

Musician Taylor Dayne decided to trade a life in Los Angeles for a slower pace in Santa Barbara after recovering from stage two colon cancer.

The “Tell It To My Heart” singer considered the move to be part of her healing process.

“I loved the idea of living in this sanctuary. It’s pretty magical up here,” she mentioned to the Montecito Journal. “I am really relishing being in a sacred space where everybody is pretty damn happy.”.

Dayne told People magazine that she’s feeling healthy four years after her diagnosis in July of this year.

It has been revealed that “So far, so good,” she said of her health. “All clean.”.

Actress Jamie Lynn Sigler was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her early 20s, and kept it private for nearly 15 years before revealing the diagnosis in 2016.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, “The Sopranos” star and her husband, Cutter Dyktra, left California with their two sons, Beau and Jack, and relocated to Texas.

“We needed a change. When I moved here, I started using a cane once in a while because I didn’t feel like I was being watched,” she told Us magazine. “Here, it was like, ‘I’m just Beau and Jack’s mom at the baseball field.’”.

The mom of two has shared that her family is fully embracing their new life.

“I feel disconnected, in the best way I’ve ever known,” she told People magazine. “It’s all about outdoors and nature which I really appreciate since I never had it growing up in Newly introduced York and L.A.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before she ever became a luxury real estate agent at The Oppenheim Group or appeared on the Netflix hit “Selling Sunset,” serial entrepreneur Emma Hernan had hired Jason Oppenheim to help her buy a home in West Hollywood, where she has since rolled out several successful businesses.

The 1940-built Colonial-style estate that Hernan bought in 2017 was a hot commodity, seeing as Oppenheim had initially hoped to snap up the property for himself, Hernan, 34, reveals to Realtor.com in the latest Celebrity Sanctuary.

“Funny enough, Jason really wanted to buy this house but he had just purchased another home, so he wanted someone that he at least knows to get it. I ended up buying it off market with Jason as my broker,” she explains.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the house hunt, Oppenheim encouraged Hernan to learn the real estate ropes so she could go from being his client to becoming his coworker and costar. After getting her real estate license in 2018, she “immediately hung [her] license with The O Group … and ended up on the show.”.

Though Hernan left “Selling Sunset” in 2025 after six seasons as a main cast member, she still works with Oppenheim and other former costars—just without the added conflict that comes with filming reality TV.

“I would describe it in one word: Peaceful,” Hernan indicates about her experience in the office now that she’s not on the show.

However, Hernan still credits the series for giving her a platform to pursue other ventures alongside luxury real estate, such as her frozen seafood and empanada brand, Coast to Coast Kitchen, which officially debuted in 2025 but had been in the works for decades.

Hernan “grew up passing out crab cakes at demos and supermarkets” because her grandfather was the founder of the Massachusetts-based seafood company, Yankee Trader Seafood. When Hernan’s mother and aunt took over and needed capital to keep the enterprise going, Hernan lent them money she had earned from modeling, nannying, and investing in the stock market.

Beyond providing funding for equipment and employees, Hernan even bought a manufacturing facility in Hingham, MA that still services her family’s tech giant as well as other food brands. She also owns a house in Norwell, MA next door to her brother’s abode, and is often in the area because of business and her boyfriend.

“Obviously, Boston is very special to me, but L.A.—I created Coast to Coast out of that kitchen with family,” she shares to illustrate why her West Coast residence holds a special place in her heart.

Industry observers note that in this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Hernan points out the potential she’s always seen in the 3,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, four-bathroom, two-story dwelling she shares with her two dogs and eight rescue cats. Plus, she opens up about how the familiar New England feel of her home kitchen helps her feed every passion.

I purchased the home in 2017 for $2.7 million and … was renting it out. I had it as an investment property because it was a bit major for me by myself. When I started filming the show, my house is super conveniently located to the office, so I moved in right when I started filming.

Recent findings suggest that this specific house and street, it's super conveniently located. It’s in the heart of West Hollywood. The office is right there. The location is a 10 for sure.

Industry observers note that there's a lot of modern homes out there. I was looking for a while and didn't fall in love with anything. Then when I walked in here, it reminded me of New England and my family's home.

Industry observers note that it was built in 1940. [The previous owners] did a small remodel [in] 1948 and then right before I purchased it, they did another small remodel, updated [the] kitchen and all that.

I redid the pool. The flooring is original and that's something that I go back and forth with changing, even though I do want to re-do the floors and warm them up. They're wood floors, original from 1940.

Recent findings suggest that the house has so much potential, which is one of the reasons why I bought it. I didn't want to buy a house that was completely done. I wanted to be able to add value and make some money off of it. I actually just had a couple contractors come by and [give a] quote.

I'm definitely gonna do a pretty major remodel. It's very home-y, but it needs updates and I'm super excited to do that. I’m gonna do the full landscaping. It needs upcoming floors, windows, all the things, but I think it'll be a really fun project.

I haven't really made it my own besides the kitchen, which I would say is my sanctuary: somewhere that feels safe, homey, and peaceful. That's really vital. My life is very public and having that peace and a place that feels home-y and safe, that's definitely what [sanctuary] means to me.

“Selling Sunset” [was] different than [selling] real estate because [reality TV is] a little bit more drama heavy, so … a lot of times when I would come home from filming, cooking and creating meals for my friends and my family really did help separate that scene that we just had that was so crazy and so hectic. Coming home and forgetting all about that, chopping the vegetables that I was gonna serve for dinner, and really being able to separate the two—I did that all in the kitchen.

The kitchen, when I bought it, was definitely one of my favorite things about the whole house. It reminded me about Latest England and my family. I added some family photos. I’m from Scituate, MA. I added this cool little Scituate plaque.

According to recent reports, it’s bright and white, but there's a lot of wood in there, too, which warms it up. Granite countertops, they're white. It's a very warm and bright kitchen. There's a lot of light that comes through. It really is my favorite part of the whole home.

The dining room area … I have a really beautiful [Restoration Hardware] dining room table that I love. And then I have this little countertop area.

It has been revealed that I've created businesses there. I’ve closed deals there. I've had family gatherings there. I’ve had Thanksgiving there, Christmas there, and so many fun little taco nights with my friends that now became my family. I’ve gone on QVC live from the kitchen. I have been in glam for “Selling Sunset.” So many of my interviews—everything's from my kitchen. It’s really special to me.

Industry observers note that the stove was literally where I created half of my recipes for Coast to Coast. So many meals are created in there. I love to cook. It's such a passion of mine. It’s therapeutic for me and that's why I was like, “I need to start my own company.

Industry observers note that I'm gonna get a fresh oven, a new SubZero, and all of that. The one thing that it's lacking is storage. I had this open space area where there's glasses, but there's not enough cabinetry, especially for the amount of cooking that I do.

In a recent development, I definitely tend to overcook because I'd rather have more than enough food than not enough. I love to cook and have many options for people. It's funny because my mom and my dad are like, “Do you need help? What do you need help with?” And I really don't need help. I love doing it. I love making every dish, making it special. I love plating it and making it look really good.

Presentation is key. I love it on a white plate, all decorative. I like everything to match. I love it to look nice, even when I'm setting up the table with nice placemats and making the table look really nice.

Some of the stuff is antique. All of my stuff in Boston was my grandmother's that was passed down. Then I've just gotten a lot of the white, classic, Crate and Barrel stuff for the L.A. [kitchen] because I'm not going to ship my really nice stuff over to L.A., especially our sentimental family pieces.

All of my guests, as soon as somebody walks in, I'm like, “What can I make you?” It doesn't matter if they're stopping over for 10 minutes. I have friends that will pop over and I’ll be like, “Do you want me to make you a sandwich? Do you want me to make you a quesadilla or throw in my empanadas?” Making people feel at home makes a difference.

What's really special about the two industries that I'm in that I genuinely love so much—it doesn't feel like work to me. I'm super grateful and I thoroughly enjoy both.

Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • Industry observers note that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

Industry observers note that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

Industry observers note that the popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” mentioned Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

According to recent reports, devRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

According to recent reports, the ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In a recent development, in September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

According to recent reports, cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin noted.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

Sources indicate that the pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

According to recent reports, in a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders remarked managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

In a recent development, experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

Recent findings suggest that “If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she mentioned. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing problem for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

According to recent reports, an agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

In a recent development, though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

It has been revealed that one is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

Sources indicate that although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Industry observers note that evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software organization went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

Recent findings suggest that if a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

According to recent reports, “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” mentioned Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Sources indicate that using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

In a recent development, cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

Recent findings suggest that “On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” remarked Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Recent findings suggest that most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

Industry observers note that “Every time a newly introduced model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” remarked Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any organization, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

According to recent reports, training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

Sources indicate that but deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” stated Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

According to recent reports, in contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” remarked David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

Recent findings suggest that “The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss stated. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

Industry observers note that performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Sources indicate that executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

According to recent reports, the corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” stated TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders remarked dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

In a recent development, sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

In a recent development, continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because newly introduced models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can swiftly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

Recent findings suggest that “Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” noted Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

According to recent reports, lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he noted. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” mentioned Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

Sources indicate that the shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., mentioned in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.

#225428. ‘We Got an Abandoned Mobile Home for Free–and Spent $14K Transforming It’

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)

‘We Got an Abandoned Mobile Home for Free–and Spent $14K Transforming It’

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.
  • But getting the home for free was only the beginning.
  • Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.

But getting the home for free was only the beginning. What followed was months of demolition, electrical and plumbing work, drywall installation, and a race to get the aging property ready for its newly introduced owner.

Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.

“I don't think I've ever had an opportunity like this before in my life, and so to turn it down would have been a shame,” Betty tells Realtor.com®. “And I know I would have regretted it, so this was probably one of the better decisions I've made in my life.”.

The family spent approximately $14,000 transforming the 1977 mobile home—a fraction of what Betty spent on rent in a year. Betty finally moved in the first week of May 2026, and now, just six months later, she is hosting her first Thanksgiving in the home her family helped bring back to life.

Lyman has worked in rental property maintenance and renovation since 2001, so he knew about the home in his small town of Irrigon, OR, that had been abandoned by the owner about five years earlier.

He discussed taking over the mobile home to renovate it and rent it out to someone in need. The landlord would be able to transfer the title to Lyman and later collect rent on the lot. Meanwhile, Lyman would be able to remove the property from the landlord’s possession.

“It was kind of like a ‘I scratch your back, you scratch my back’ kind of deal,” Branson tells Realtor.com.

Initially, Lyman saw the renovation as another project for his YouTube channel, which he rolled out in early 2025. But the timing was also opportune for his sister, whose living circumstances had unexpectedly changed just days before he called.

Sources indicate that betty had been searching for another rental and considered buying an RV, paying approximately $800 a month for space at an RV park. Instead, her brother presented her with an opportunity to finally own a place of her own.

Betty could contribute what her brother calls “sweat equity,” working on the property before and after her regular job.

The purchase price was zero, but the property was far from move-in ready. The floors and walls were rotted, and there were leaks, water damage, and missing sections of ceiling.

“Basically, it was ready for the dump,” Lyman indicates.

With more than two decades of experience in the industry, he recognized that the structure was salvageable and the renovation worthwhile. Betty, however, was less convinced.

“I was a little overwhelmed and kind of scared when I first saw it,” she recalls.

She saw the home's many problems, including the broken countertop and the hole in the wall where a window would later be installed.

The home remained in its original location, eliminating the expense of transporting it. However, it was still sitting on flat tires and had never been properly set up. So the family's first task was to stabilize the structure on blocks.

Industry observers note that the landlord waived the lot rent for six months while the family obtained the necessary permits. Renovation began in October 2025. Lyman and his father, with help from other family members, updated the almost 50-year-old mobile home to current building codes.

They replaced broken flooring, added insulation and drywall, and wrapped the outside of the home to protect it from the elements. Lyman shared the process on his YouTube channel.

Walls were painted, the bathroom drywall was finished, and the overall interior was beginning to look like a home. But the project wasn't without setbacks.

“There were a couple times that I was still in the middle of it all, and I'm like, 'We're too far in. I can't quit now,'” Betty recalls. “But this is hard and this is scary.”.

She had to depend on her brother and her father for help when various issues arose during the renovation.

“I'm so grateful because without them, this wouldn't have been possible for me,”  she says.

Betty received her certificate of occupancy two weeks before the permit expired.

“I was actually really amazed that we were able to make it in the time frame that we did with how much that was done,” she says.

Sources indicate that the renovation offered Betty something she had never experienced in 20 years of renting. She got to design the layout of her living space. She got to pick out the locations of her light switches and outlets. Her daughters, who share a bedroom, chose paint colors and the arrangement for the closets.

“It was an experience for me that I'll never forget,” Betty notes.

The renovation of the free mobile home came with substantial expenses.

LeAnna Branson, Lyman and Betty's mother, who kept track of the receipts for the renovation, tells Realtor.com that the family initially budgeted between $10,000 and $12,000. However, rising material costs, unexpected damage discovered during demolition, and decisions to upgrade certain features pushed the total to approximately $14,000.

Betty also opted to spend a little more on higher-quality materials and finishes, knowing she intended to live there for years.

“I could have gone cheaper. Definitely, we could have cut some costs here and there,” she says. “But I proposal to be here for a while. I want it to last.”.

It has been revealed that betty used her savings to kick-start the renovation and lived in her sister’s RV, which allowed her to devote her income to the renovation for six months. Once she moved in and began paying rent on the lot, plus utilities, the pace of the work slowed a bit.

Sources indicate that now, Lyman estimates the renovation is approximately 90% complete. The remaining work involves the upper kitchen cabinets, wall tile, a window replacement, and several finishing touches.

It has been revealed that the family also received support from viewers of Lyman's YouTube channel, who contributed an estimated $1,000 to $2,000. Even the handles that will adorn Betty's kitchen cabinets and drawers were paid for by a viewer.

Industry observers note that “More support than I ever imagined,” Lyman indicates of the response to the project. His viewers “loved seeing the family aspect.”.

For Betty, the financial benefits extend well beyond the renovation costs. She notes she has more living space than she would have gotten in an apartment. And there's space for her daughters and her dog.

Industry observers note that “We went over budget a little, but considering [Betty] was paying $20,000 a year to rent, $14,000 is not that bad,” LeAnna says. “I mean it's a chunk of money, but it's doable.”.

Lyman believes owning a mobile home, even when you must rent the land it sits on, can offer an affordable housing alternative to people struggling to keep up with rising rental costs across the country.

“That was important for Betty as well, so that she could afford to live the life she deserves,” he says.

Though Betty’s experience shows that acquiring a free or inexpensive mobile home is only a small part of the financial equation, her brother’s professional experience, the family’s help, and the landlord’s willingness to waive her lot rent during the renovation also helped keep costs manageable.

For her parents, seeing their daughter choose everything from her kitchen sink to her bathroom tile was particularly rewarding.

“It gave us a peace of mind to know, you know, that she finally has a place of her own to call her home,” her mother claims.

Sources indicate that some of the most special features of her new home are things visitors won’t see. Behind her new cupboards are messages from her family who helped her renovate her home.

“I have places on the wall behind some of the cupboards where the family all, like, signed their names and left me love notes,” Betty says. “I know they're there, even though some of them are covered up.”.

The transformation is a daily reminder of what her family made possible.

Sources indicate that “The fact that it was my family that assisted me along the way makes it even more special,” she states. “It wasn't just hiring outside help, but family and friends that came to put in the time and effort that they could to help. It makes it mean so much more to me.”.

Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts that Bitcoin is quietly setting the stage for a move that could rewrite every previous cycle high by early 2027.

Despite heavy selling pressure, persistent ETF outflows, and extreme fear that has dominated recent weeks, a handful of structural developments are emerging beneath the noise.

The real catalyst capable of flipping the entire narrative, however, remains highly unlikely yet not impossible: a coordinated announcement in which several G20 nations and major sovereign wealth funds simultaneously designate Bitcoin as a core strategic reserve asset.

It would commit to multi-year accumulation programs totaling hundreds of thousands of BTC while integrating it into cross-border settlement systems for tokenized trade and energy markets.

Such a step would instantly transform Bitcoin from a speculative asset into a recognized monetary reserve, triggering a supply shock of historic proportions.

Industry observers note that crypto is up today as Bitcoin reclaimed the $60,000 level and major altcoins followed higher in a broad relief rally. Bitcoin climbed roughly 2–3.5% to trade around $60,600–$60,900, while Ethereum gained about 2–4% near $1,700. XRP, Solana, and Dogecoin also advanced 2.5%-4%.

In a recent development, the total crypto market capitalization rose approximately 2–3% to around $2.1 trillion. Several factors drove the move. Prices had become deeply oversold after recent declines toward the mid-$50,000s for Bitcoin, attracting dip buyers and triggering short liquidations that amplified the upside.

Industry observers note that risk assets more broadly recovered, with technology and AI-related stocks providing a supportive backdrop that spilled over into crypto given their high correlation. Thin holiday trading volumes ahead of Thanksgiving also contributed to sharper moves.

Sentiment received a modest lift from progress on a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill that cleared a House committee. Despite ongoing heavy ETF outflows and extreme fear readings near 11 on the Fear & Greed Index, technical oversold conditions, forced short covering, and improving risk appetite fueled today’s rebound.

On higher timeframes, Bitcoin has undergone a substantial correction from its previous cycle peaks, carving out a series of lower highs while finding repeated support in the mid-$50,000s to low-$60,000s.

The recent stabilization above $58,000–$60,000 after a sharp liquidation-driven flush has produced the first meaningful higher low on the weekly chart in several months.

Volume on the recovery legs has modestly expanded relative to the preceding decline, and weekly RSI has begun to diverge positively from the price lows, moving out of deeply oversold territory.

Key resistance remains clustered between $65,000 and $72,000; a decisive weekly close above that zone would confirm that the multi-month downtrend is exhausting itself.

With a true demand shock, measured-move projections and multi-year Fibonacci extensions from the current base open the door to far higher valuations once price enters a newly introduced discovery phase.

Against a backdrop of extreme fear and heavy outflows, the market is precisely where long-term asymmetric opportunities historically appear.

Residual institutional accumulation, legislative progress on national reserves, and a still-intact long-term supply-scarcity narrative provide the foundation for a powerful reversal if the right catalyst arrives.

Even amid record November ETF outflows exceeding $5Bn and elevated rate-hike odds, several constructive signals have emerged.

Industry observers note that the House Financial Services Committee advanced legislation to formalize a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve with a long-term lock-up provision, keeping the institutional adoption story alive.

Morgan Stanley has continued expanding its Bitcoin ETF exposure, and Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) remains a steadfast large-scale holder.

Broader market rebounds, including the relief rally following Nvidia’s leadership clarity, have helped Bitcoin reclaim the $60,000 level after testing multi-month lows.

Regulatory progress in other jurisdictions, such as Ukraine’s legalization framework, adds incremental legitimacy. These developments don’t erase near-term headwinds, but they show institutional interest hasn’t disappeared; it is simply waiting for clearer macro conditions.

If the hypothetical sovereign-reserve adoption wave materializes in late 2026, Bitcoin could accelerate far beyond previous expectations.

By January 1, 2027, Claude AI predicts its over-the-top scenario supports a target range of $285,000 to $375,000, with an aggressive stretch objective above $450,000.
